And when `FruDevice` instance goes out of scope we are already at the point where `fruDevice.io.run()` returns so there should not be any other code running beyond that point.

I am kind of stuck here as from a local reasoning perspective your suggestion is better but i would like to avoid introducing any `shared_ptr` for `FruDevice` instance since we know it's lifetime already (thus no need for `shared_ptr`).

So both choices are wrong and because of that i would like to go with the simpler choice (no `shared_ptr`).

~> singleton.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singleton_pattern

> In object-oriented programming, the singleton pattern is a software design pattern that restricts the instantiation of a class to a singular instance

I did not put a mechanism in the class to enforce it as singleton because i consider it to be obvious from looking at the usage within the application context.


> Right... this is the point, there's no guarantee of this within the class, which leads to subtle bugs. FWIW, that's somewhat why these were globals initially and not on stack.

And global vars accessible from any function which can see them does not lead to subtle bugs?

> Right... this is the point, there's no guarantee of this within the class, which leads to subtle bugs. FWIW, that's somewhat why these were globals initially and not on stack.

Yes, there can be problems with classes that we do not have with globals.

I got one such issue in testing when `std::bind_front` was implicitly copy constructing the bus map.

Changed the code now to make the classes non-copyable and non-moveable.

This solidifies their role as singletons in the application context.
I hope this resolves your concern 👍

Initially it was not a shared pointer, i made it a shared pointer based on feedback

https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/entity-manager/+/84123/comment/702f91e9_fb2b3786/

From what i remember the concern there was local reasoning. If we pass in a reference to FruDevice into some function, the lifetime is not known when looking only at that one function. So if we want to use that reference later as part of a callback or something then it would have to be passed in as shared_ptr.

So even if we know (from global reasoning) about the lifetime of FruDevice instance, we cannot use that information since it is preferred to be able to understand/review a single function separately.

Even though the inline lambda for `ReScan` is technically a separate function, the reader is still inside `main` function. So we can use local reasoning and see that the FruDevice instance is in scope from line 1328 until the end of `main` function.

So from my perspective it is fine to leave it like this for now, unless someone has a strong opinion here. Do you think it should be changed?

I think you have an object that owns itself here.

From my perspective

- scan is constructed
- scan constructor stores shared_ptr<FruDevice>
- scan destructor is called
- `_callback()` is called
- `scan->run()` is called
- `fruDevice->findI2CDevices` does it's thing and hopefully returns
- `scan->run()` returns 
- `_callback()` returns
- `scan destructor returns`


So while the `FruDevice` instance may be kept alive by whoever called it's functions here, i don't think `struct FindDevicesWithCallback` can rely on that,
so it gets it's own shared_ptr to FruDevice.
